items.abstract: <jats:p>Developing embodied AI systems that interpret free-form natural language and execute appropriate manipulation actions in cluttered environments remains a central challenge in multimodal decision- making. Existing language-conditioned grasping methods typically accommodate only a single instruction granularity (e.g., object names), which limits their capacity to resolve ambiguity when multiple semantically similar objects coexist. We present GraspMind, a multimodal expert framework for multi-granularity language-conditioned affordance prediction that accommodates instructions across six levels of specificity: object category, visual attribute, spatial relation, functional purpose, part-level reference, and their combinations. GraspMind couples a frozen CLIP text encoder with a PointNet++ 3D backbone through cross-attention fusion, enabling per-point alignment between linguistic semantics and geometric features while producing interpretable word-level attention maps that explicate the system’s decision rationale. To prevent shortcut learning in multi-object settings, we propose the Instruction-Aware Scene Curriculum (IASC), a principled data generation strategy that constructs adversarial scenes containing granularity-specific distractors by decomposing each instruction into discriminative and confounding semantic dimensions. Comprehensive experiments conducted in ManiSkill3/SAPIEN with YCB objects demonstrate that GraspMind achieves strong affordance prediction on object, attribute, spatial, and functional instructions, with IASC contributing a 40% relative improvement over random scene compositions. We further evaluate robustness to sensor noise, open-vocabulary generalization, and multi-seed consistency, identifying part-level and mixed-granularity instructions as open challenges that necessitate richer input modalities. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GraspMind-8330/.</jats:p>
title: GraspMind: Multi-Granularity Language-Conditioned Affordance Prediction for Robotic Grasping

items.abstract: <jats:p>Solubility prediction across temperature is crucial for solvent selection and process design, yet remains challenging for data-driven models because temperature is typically treated as a simple scalar input. Such treatment limits the ability of data-driven methods to represent temperature-dependent solute–solvent interactions within their latent feature spaces. Here, we introduce a temperature-conditioned (T-conditioned) molecular representation that embeds temperature directly into learned features through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) after dimension expansion. We evaluate this approach using two representative solubility prediction architectures: Chemprop, based on learned graph-based representations, and Fastprop, based on fixed descriptors. Trained on BigSolDB and assessed under both interpolation and extrapolation to unseen solutes using the Leeds and SolProp datasets, Tconditioning consistently reduces prediction error by up to 38% for Chemprop, with particularly strong improvements at elevated temperatures (up to 51% RMSE reduction above 330 K), while gains for Fastprop remain modest. Analysis of the T-conditioning parameters reveals that temperature-dependent modulation increases with temperature, indicating that the T-conditioning layer captures temperature-sensitive latent features relevant to solubility. An application study on pyrazinamide solubility prediction further demonstrates improved agreement with experimental trends and highlights the utility of representation-level conditioning when mechanistic models are constrained by parameters. These results demonstrate that T-conditioning enables accurate and physically meaningful prediction of temperature-dependent properties by embedding temperature directly into molecular representations.</jats:p>
title: Temperature-conditioned molecular representation for organic solubility prediction

items.abstract: <jats:p>Temporal link prediction with temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) is increasingly used to model spatio-temporal dependencies in temporal graphs and to forecast future interactions among entities. Existing sampling-based training methods typically rely on random negative sampling and pointwise loss formulations, which often lead to suboptimal convergence and limited generalization due to low-quality negative samples. We propose ATNSF, a temporal graph learning framework with a hybrid negative sampling strategy that uses a portion of historical edges as hard negatives. For efficiency, we design an asynchronous parallel training pipeline for scalable optimization and introduce a pairwise sampled softmax loss that contrasts each positive instance with a batch of negatives to learn more discriminative representations. Finally, we theoretically show that jointly designing the loss function and negative sampling strategy is crucial for improving performance and generalization. Extensive experiments across six temporal graph datasets demonstrate that ATNSF improves the average AP from 0.724 to 0.827 (+0.103). Remarkably, it also accelerates training by 1.37× to 6.85×, achieving a 2.57× geometric mean speedup. The source code of this paper can be found at https://github.com/yongqiu-star/ATNSF.</jats:p>
title: History Doesn’t Repeat, but Its Patterns Echo: A Parallel Pairwise Negative-Sampling Framework for Temporal Link Prediction

items.abstract:
<jats:p>Since the beginnings of social and behavioural sciences, the link prediction problem has 
<br>
 grabbed much attention. 
<br>
 For instance, social networks such as Facebook, Twitter, and LinkedIN change enduringly as 
<br>
 new connections appear in the graph. For these networks, one of the biggest challenges is to 
<br>
 find accurately the best recommendations to the users. 
<br>
 Within the meaning of the graph, the main objective of the link prediction problem is to 
<br>
 predict the upcoming links from the actual state of a graph. 
<br>
 Link prediction methods use some score functions, such as 
<br>
 ● Jaccard coefficient 
<br>
 ● Preferential attachment, 
<br>
 to measure the probability of adding the links to the network. 
<br>
 These metrics are widely used in various applications due to their simplicity and their 
<br>
 interpretability; however, the majority of them are designed for a specific domain. 
<br>
 Social networks become very large with a several number of users that are connected with 
<br>
 different kinds of links. 
<br>
 Predicting those links is still a challenging task, as we need to find the best way to perform 
<br>
 predictions as accurate as possible.</jats:p>
title: Evaluation Of Link Prediction Techniques

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Hypermobile Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (hEDS), postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) are reported to co-occur frequently. It is unclear how strongly, whether symptom profiles sharpen prediction of a second diagnosis given a first, and whether the published literature can support such inference at all.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We pooled 22 published cohorts—aggregate prevalence data, no primary human-subjects data—using Bayesian hierarchical random-effects models on the logit scale, and propagated the resulting posteriors through naive and tempered symptom updating. We introduce a feasibility screen derived from the Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds that tests whether separately pooled marginals can describe a single population, and we characterise the identifiability of latent class structure under disease-selected sampling.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Directed comorbidity is strongly asymmetric:
                    <jats:italic>π</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>POTS|hEDS</jats:sub>
                    = 46.6% (95% CrI [32.5, 61.5]) against
                    <jats:italic>π</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>hEDS|POTS</jats:sub>
                    = 12.1% ([3.5, 38.5]), a near-fourfold gap, with
                    <jats:italic>π</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>MCAS|POTS</jats:sub>
                    lowest at 3.9% ([0.7, 21.6]). Prediction intervals exceed credible intervals throughout, indicating substantial between-cohort heterogeneity. The feasibility screen finds 26 of 102 testable cells (25.5%) incompatible with
                    <jats:italic>any</jats:italic>
                    joint distribution; critically, 21 of these fail the upper Fréchet bound and are invisible to the one-sided screen that is the natural first implementation. Among cells surviving the screen, symptom evidence is informative in four of six directions—ℙ(hEDS|POTS,
                    <jats:bold>S</jats:bold>
                    ) rises from 12.1% to 49.7% on a four-symptom panel under tempered updating, and ℙ(POTS|MCAS,
                    <jats:bold>S</jats:bold>
                    ) from 49.5% to 82.1%—but inert in both hEDS-cohort directions. A pathway-dispersion contrast excludes zero in two of six directions, in opposite signs and by margins of 0.1–0.2 percentage points, consistent with chance at this number of comparisons. We show latent class structure is not identified from disease-selected aggregate data, and that the single cohort reporting trivariate structure (
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                    = 8) yields an exactly balanced table (OR = 1.00, 95% CI [0.063, 15.99]).
                  </jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The pooled directional probabilities are usable as clinical priors, with intervals wide enough to preclude precision. Symptom-conditioned prediction is supported in some directions but not those most often invoked clinically, and every estimate rests on cohorts dominated by self-reported ascertainment. The principal methodological contribution is the two-sided feasibility screen: applied here it shows that a quarter of the testable literature cannot describe one coherent population, and that a one-sided implementation understates this sixfold.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
title: Symptom-conditioned prediction of comorbidity in the hEDS–POTS–MCAS triad

items.abstract: <jats:p>Aeroacoustic source attribution is often visualized as a local source map, but a locally intense source need not be important to a specified observer. It may be nearly silent after propagation, cancel another source coherently, or represent deterministic conversion of pre-existing entropy or vortical content rather than fresh emission. We formulate source attribution as an observer-conditioned stochastic covariance problem. Mechanism-resolved source channels are mapped to an outgoing detector through a positive-semidefinite radiativity operator $K_\Theta$. Deterministic observer power is a bilinear form, $\Pi_\Theta=S^\dagger K_\Theta S$, while stochastic observer power is the trace budget $\E\Pi_\Theta=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\tr(K^\Theta_{\beta\alpha}\Phi_{\alpha\beta})$, where $\Phi_{\alpha\beta}$ is the cross-spectral covariance between source channels. The formulation preserves self-radiation, cross-channel interference, cancellation, and observer dependence. A controlled verification and demonstration ladder is developed using two-patch Helmholtz radiation, a direct full-state quasi-one-dimensional nozzle case with direct and indirect noise, a compressed hidden-observable identifiability test, a direct full-state moving-shock-layer case, and a radiation-aware covariance-closure study with prior-mismatch, noise, observer-sparsity, and multiple-truth ablations. The results show that radiating importance is not equivalent to source energy: energy-ranked low-rank models can capture high-variance but nearly silent directions, whereas observer-radiativity-ranked models recover held-out observer powers and channel budgets at much lower rank. The framework replaces a universal local radiating-source density by an interference-aware source-to-observer covariance budget.</jats:p>
title: Observer-conditioned stochastic source attribution for compressible aeroacoustics
